name: Physics
title: Mars Rescue
description: Power a rover, plan its route, and get the crew home.
intro: A rover is stranded on Mars. Let's use force, speed, and energy to bring it home.

questions.title: Get the rover moving
questions.scene: The 10 kg rover needs an acceleration of 2 m/s². Ignore friction for this challenge.
questions.question: How much net force does it need?
questions.hint: Force is mass multiplied by acceleration. Use 10 kg and 2 m/s².
questions.concept: Newton's second law connects net force, mass, and acceleration: F = ma. A larger mass needs more force for the same acceleration.
questions.explanation: 10 × 2 = 20 N. The rover can now accelerate toward the crew.

questions.title: Reach the landing zone
questions.scene: The rover travels 120 meters in 30 seconds.
questions.question: What is its average speed?
questions.hint: Divide the total distance by the total time. Keep meters on top and seconds underneath.
questions.concept: Average speed measures the total distance traveled per unit of time. It does not tell us the rover's speed at every moment.
questions.explanation: 120 ÷ 30 = 4 m/s. You've worked out how quickly the rover reached the landing zone.

questions.title: Charge the rescue beacon
questions.scene: A 20 W beacon runs for 5 seconds.
questions.question: How much energy does it use?
questions.hint: A watt is one joule per second. Multiply the power by how many seconds the beacon runs.
questions.concept: Power is the rate of energy transfer. Multiplying power in watts by time in seconds gives energy in joules.
questions.explanation: 20 × 5 = 100 J. The beacon is online and the rescue crew has your signal.

name: Calculus
title: Reactor Run
description: Read changing signals and bring a reactor back online.
intro: The reactor's signals keep changing. We'll use derivatives and integrals to understand them.

questions.title: Read the changing signal
questions.scene: A sensor reports f(x) = x². You need its rate of change at x = 3.
questions.question: What is f′(3)?
questions.hint: First find the derivative of x² using the power rule. Then put 3 into that new expression.
questions.concept: A derivative gives an instantaneous rate of change. With the power rule, the exponent becomes a multiplier and the exponent decreases by one.
questions.explanation: The derivative of x² is 2x. At x = 3, 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.title: Count the stored energy
questions.scene: The rate of energy transfer is P(t) = 2t watts for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 seconds.
questions.question: How much energy is transferred over those two seconds?
questions.hint: An antiderivative of 2t is t². Evaluate it at the upper and lower time limits, then subtract.
questions.concept: A definite integral adds up a changing rate over an interval. Integrating power over time gives the total energy transferred.

questions.title: Spot the steady signal
questions.scene: A temperature signal is constant: T(t) = 7.
questions.question: What is its rate of change?
questions.hint: Think about the slope of a horizontal line. Does its height change as time moves forward?
questions.concept: The derivative of a constant is zero because the value does not change. A flat signal has no upward or downward slope.
questions.explanation: The temperature stays at 7, so its rate of change is 0. The reactor's final signal is stable.

name: Biopharma Cyber Detective
title: The Helix Breach
description: Follow the evidence and uncover an altered lab dataset.
intro: A fictional lab's dataset was changed. Let's compare the evidence carefully and find the altered record.

questions.title: Check the DNA rules
questions.scene: Before examining the dataset, you check the standard base pairs in DNA.
questions.question: Which base normally pairs with adenine (A) in DNA?
questions.hint: The usual DNA pairs are A–T and C–G. Match the full base name to its letter.
questions.concept: Complementary DNA strands normally pair adenine with thymine and cytosine with guanine. These pairings help us compare sequence records.
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine in DNA. You now have the base-pair rule for checking the record.

questions.title: Compare the records
questions.scene: In this fictional case, the verified record has C–G at locus 734. The exported record has T–A at that same locus.
questions.question: Which change is actually supported by the evidence?
questions.hint: Compare the same locus in both records. Follow what the records show rather than guessing from a packet ID.
questions.concept: A supported finding compares matching locations in a trusted record and the record under investigation. A matching identifier alone would not prove a change.
questions.explanation: Both records refer to locus 734, where C–G became T–A. That comparison supports the finding that this exported record differs.

questions.title: Protect the evidence
questions.scene: You need to detect whether a saved evidence file changes during your investigation.
questions.question: Which action helps verify the file's integrity?
options: Take a screenshot of the filename
Record and compare its SHA-256 hash
questions.hint: Look for a method tied to the file's contents. A name or screenshot does not verify every byte.
questions.concept: A cryptographic hash is a fingerprint of file contents. Comparing it with a trusted earlier hash helps detect changes; it does not prove who created the file.
questions.explanation: Record the SHA-256 hash and compare it later against the trusted value. You've identified the changed record and protected your evidence.
